entry: Ethical and moral codes taught by religious traditions. Examples of religiously derived legal codes include Christian canon law, Jewish [[Halakha]], Islamic [[Sharia|sharia]] and Hindu law. In some jurisdictions, religious law applies only to that religion's adherents; in others, civil authorities may enforce it for all residents. A [[State religion|state religion]] is a religious body officially endorsed by the state. A [[Theocracy|theocracy]] is a government in which a god or deity is recognized as the supreme civil ruler. In Buddhism, the Patimokkha is a code of 227 rules and principles followed by monks and nuns. In [[Christianity]], the Mosaic Law, which Christians take from the [[Old Testament|Old Testament]], is also called divine or biblical law; the [[Ten Commandments]] are its most famous example. Some Christian denominations contrast law with grace, the contrast speaking to an attempt to gain [[Salvation|salvation]] by obedience to a code of laws rather than through faith.

Study of religion from a historical or scientific perspective. Religious studies, also known as religiology, describes, compares, interprets and explains religion using empirical, historically based and cross-cultural perspectives. Unlike [[Theology|theology]], which seeks to understand the transcendent or [[Supernatural|supernatural]] according to traditional religious accounts, it takes a more scientific and objective approach, independent of any particular religious viewpoint. The discipline draws on anthropology, [[Sociology|sociology]], psychology, philosophy and the history of religion. It originated in 19th-century Europe, when biblical scholarship flourished and Hindu and Buddhist sacred texts were first translated into European languages. Early scholars included Friedrich Max Müller and Cornelis Petrus Tiele. In the United States, the field has also been called "History of religion," a name associated with the [[University of Chicago]]. Some argue that studying religion helps in understanding sectarian tensions and religious violence.

A [[War|war]] primarily caused or justified by differences in [[Religion|religion]] and beliefs, sometimes called a holy war (Latin: *sanctum bellum*). Historians debate the extent to which religious, economic, ethnic or political factors predominate in a given conflict. Some scholars argue that the idea of religious war is a largely Western dichotomy and a modern invention, while others, such as Jeffrey Burton Russell, suggest that religion may mask underlying secular power and economic reasons. According to the *Encyclopedia of Wars*, religion was the primary cause of 121 of 1,763 known historical conflicts, or 6.87%. Matthew White's *The Great Big Book of Horrible Things* gives religion as the primary cause of 11 of the world's 100 deadliest atrocities. Historians generally do not accept that religions are more violent or cause most wars. Konrad Repgen argued that a war is religious when at least one belligerent claims a religious law to justify it.

Memorial day observed in former countries of the [[British Empire|British Empire]] and current [[Commonwealth of Nations|Commonwealth]] member states, also known as Poppy Day. It honors armed forces members who died in the line of duty. Most countries observe it on November 11, to recall the end of First World War hostilities in 1918. The tradition evolved from [[Armistice Day]], which was first observed at [[Buckingham Palace]] in 1919 under [[George V|King George V]]. After the Second World War, Commonwealth states adopted the name Remembrance Day, while the United States chose Veterans Day.

Family (Echeneidae) of ray-finned fish, sometimes called suckerfish or sharksucker. Remoras grow to 30–110 cm (12–43 in) long, depending on species. Their first dorsal fin forms a modified oval, sucker-like organ that attaches them to larger marine animals, including [[Shark|sharks]], [[Manta ray|manta rays]], [[Whale|whales]] and [[Turtle|turtles]]. Remoras are tropical open-ocean dwellers, but they occasionally occur in temperate or coastal waters. Smaller remoras also fasten onto [[Tuna|tuna]] and [[Swordfish|swordfish]]. A host relationship is most often classed as commensalism, though some are mutualistic: remoras can remove ectoparasites and loose skin while benefiting from their host's protection and the water flowing over their gills. Dolphins with attached remoras are believed not to benefit, because the attachment increases [[Drag (physics)|drag]].

Electronic device used to operate another device from a distance, usually wirelessly. In [[Consumer electronics|consumer electronics]], remote controls operate [[Television|televisions]], [[DVD]] players and other home media appliances. Early television remote controls, from 1956 to 1977, used ultrasonic tones. Most present-day remotes are [[Infrared|infrared]] devices that send digitally coded pulses, and universal remotes can emulate the codes of most major brands. Wired and wireless remote control was developed in the late 19th century to guide unmanned vehicles, mainly military [[Torpedo|torpedoes]]. [[Nikola Tesla]] also demonstrated a prototype in New York in 1898. The Philco Mystery Control of 1939 was the first wireless remote control for a consumer electronics device. In the 2000s, remotes included [[Bluetooth|Bluetooth]] or [[Wi-Fi|Wi-Fi]] connectivity, motion sensors and voice control.

Acquisition of information about an object or area from a distance, without touching it. The term usually refers to observing [[Earth|Earth]] from [[Satellite|satellites]] or aircraft, but it also covers ship- or ground-based methods such as [[Sonar|sonar]]. It is used in [[Geophysics|geophysics]], [[Geography|geography]], land surveying and most [[Earth science|Earth science]] disciplines. Passive sensors record naturally emitted or reflected energy, most often [[Sunlight|sunlight]] reflected from a surface. Active sensors supply their own energy, and [[Radar|radar]] and lidar time the interval between sending a pulse and receiving its return, which gives the distance to the target. Brazil's National Institute for Space Research has measured deforestation in the Amazon Basin every year since 1988 using Landsat-class imagery. Satellite altimetry combined with moored buoys is used to track El Niño.

Belgian [[Surrealism|surrealist]] painter. His works show familiar objects in unfamiliar, unexpected settings, which often provoked questions about the nature and boundaries of reality and representation. He began as an Impressionist, and the paintings he made between 1918 and 1924 were influenced by [[Futurism|Futurism]] and [[Cubism|Cubism]]. He held his first solo exhibition in [[Brussels|Brussels]] in 1927, then moved to Paris, where he befriended André Breton and became involved with the Surrealist group. He returned to Brussels in 1930 and resumed work in advertising. His imagery influenced [[Pop art|pop art]], minimalist art and [[Conceptual art|conceptual art]]. Notable works include *The Treachery of Images* (1929).

American actress. She won two [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]]: Best Supporting Actress for *Cold Mountain* (2003) and Best Actress for *Judy* (2019), in which she played [[Judy Garland|Judy Garland]]. Born and raised in [[Texas|Texas]], she studied [[English literature|English literature]] at the University of Texas at Austin. Her films include *Jerry Maguire* (1996), *Bridget Jones's Diary* (2001) and *Chicago* (2002). In 2022 she starred as Pam Hupp in the [[NBC|NBC]] miniseries *The Thing About Pam*.

European architectural style of the early 15th to early 16th centuries, which revived elements of ancient Greek and Roman architecture. It followed [[Gothic architecture|Gothic architecture]] and was succeeded by [[Baroque architecture|Baroque]] and neoclassical styles. The style developed first in [[Florence|Florence]], where [[Filippo Brunelleschi|Filippo Brunelleschi]] was one of its innovators, before spreading to other Italian cities and to France, Spain and the Low Countries. It emphasized [[Symmetry|symmetry]], proportion and geometry, with orderly columns, pilasters and lintels, semicircular arches, hemispherical [[Dome|domes]] and niches. Wealthy patrons, including the Medici family and the Catholic Church, commissioned buildings that displayed religious devotion and political power. Architects such as Brunelleschi, [[Leon Battista Alberti|Leon Battista Alberti]] and later [[Andrea Palladio|Andrea Palladio]] reshaped urban landscapes with domes, columns and harmonious facades.

Painting, sculpture and decorative arts of the European [[Renaissance|Renaissance]], which emerged as a distinct style in [[Italy|Italy]] around AD 1400. It took as its foundation the art of [[Classical antiquity|Classical antiquity]], while absorbing recent developments in Northern European art and applying contemporary scientific knowledge. Most of it was produced during the 14th, 15th and 16th centuries, under the influence of growing interest in nature, a revival of classical learning and a more individualistic view of humanity. The Medici Bank brought unprecedented wealth to [[Florence|Florence]], and [[Cosimo de' Medici|Cosimo de' Medici]] set a new standard for patronage of the arts that was not associated with the church or monarchy. Movable-type [[Printing|printing]] in the 15th century allowed ideas to spread widely. Classical forms appeared in painting and sculpture as early as the 1420s, in the work of [[Masaccio|Masaccio]] and Uccello, and oil paint was improved by artists such as [[Jan van Eyck|Jan van Eyck]].

European musical period of the 15th and 16th centuries. Music became increasingly free of medieval constraints and a vehicle for personal expression, as composers made vocal music more expressive of its texts. Textures were rich, with four or more independent melodic parts performed at once, a style called polyphony. Early in the period, [[Guillaume Du Fay|Guillaume Du Fay]] cultivated the cantilena style; the middle period was dominated by the Franco-Flemish school and [[Josquin des Prez|Josquin des Prez]]. The period culminated during the [[Counter-Reformation|Counter-Reformation]] in the florid [[Counterpoint|counterpoint]] of [[Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina|Palestrina]]. Precursors of instruments including the [[Lute|lute]] developed into new forms, and early forms of the [[Bassoon|bassoon]] and [[Trombone|trombone]] appeared. Toward the end of the 16th century, church modes began to give way to functional tonality.

Philosophical thought of the European [[Renaissance|Renaissance]], roughly 1400 to 1600. It overlaps with late [[Medieval philosophy|medieval philosophy]], which was influenced by figures such as [[Thomas Aquinas|Thomas Aquinas]] and [[William of Ockham|William of Ockham]], and with early modern philosophy, which conventionally begins with [[René Descartes|René Descartes]] and his *Discourse on Method* (1637). Renaissance philosophy kept much of the structure, sources and methods of earlier centuries. [[Aristotle|Aristotle]] remained foundational, and his [[Nicomachean Ethics|Nicomachean Ethics]] was the main authority for ethics at Protestant universities until the late 17th century. Scholars continued the scholastic method of disputed questions, and Pico della Mirandola's *Disputations* depended directly on this tradition.

French multinational automobile manufacturer, founded in 1899 as Société Renault Frères by Louis Renault and his brothers Marcel and Fernand. It is headquartered in Boulogne-Billancourt, near [[Paris|Paris]], and has previously made [[Truck|trucks]], [[Tractor|tractors]], [[Tank|tanks]], [[Bus|buses]] and [[Aircraft|aircraft]]. The group has been part of the Renault–Nissan–Mitsubishi Alliance since 1999. Renault is known for motor sport, particularly rallying, [[Formula One|Formula One]] and Formula E. Its early work on mathematical curve modeling for car bodies is significant in the history of [[Computer graphics|computer graphics]].

Official currency of the [[China|People's Republic of China]], issued by the People's Bank of China. The base unit is the yuan, divided into 10 jiao or 100 fen; fen coins are now rarely used because of [[Inflation|inflation]]. The renminbi is the world's fifth-most-traded currency as of April 2025. Until 2005 its [[Exchange rate|exchange rate]] was pegged to the U.S. dollar, and since 2006 it has been allowed to float within a narrow margin around a base rate set against a basket of world currencies. In 2011 the [[International Monetary Fund|International Monetary Fund]] stated that the renminbi was undervalued by 23%. On October 1, 2016, it became the first emerging market currency in the IMF's special drawing rights basket, with an initial weighting of 10.9%. Because the yuan symbol ¥ is also used for the [[Japanese yen|Japanese yen]], RMB is written when a distinction is needed.

City in northwestern [[Nevada|Nevada]], on the California border, and the county seat of Washoe County. It had a population of 264,165 at the 2020 census and is known as "The Biggest Little City in the World." The city is named after Union major general Jesse L. Reno, who was killed in the [[American Civil War|American Civil War]]. For much of the 20th century, Reno had a national reputation as a divorce mill under Nevada's relatively lax laws. Today it is a tourist destination known for [[Casino|casino]] gambling. The University of Nevada at Reno is its flagship campus.

Rock musical with music, lyrics and book by [[Jonathan Larson|Jonathan Larson]], loosely based on [[Giacomo Puccini|Puccini]]'s opera *La bohème*. It follows impoverished young artists in the East Village of [[Manhattan|Manhattan]], under the shadow of [[HIV/AIDS|HIV/AIDS]]. Larson had died suddenly the night before its off-Broadway performances began on January 26, 1996. The show moved to Broadway on April 29, 1996, and won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama and the Tony Award for Best Musical. It closed in 2008 after 12 years and had grossed over $280 million. A motion picture adaptation appeared in 2005.

Branch of mathematics that studies abstract algebraic structures by representing their elements as linear transformations of [[Vector space|vector spaces]]. Elements of an abstract object are described by [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] and their operations, which makes the object more concrete. The method applies to [[Group (mathematics)|groups]], associative algebras and Lie algebras. It reduces problems in [[Abstract algebra|abstract algebra]] to problems in [[Linear algebra|linear algebra]], a well-understood subject. Representing a group on an infinite-dimensional [[Hilbert space|Hilbert space]] allows methods of analysis to be applied to the theory of groups. In [[Physics|physics]], it describes how the symmetry group of a physical system affects the solutions of the equations describing it. It also generalizes [[Fourier analysis|Fourier analysis]] and has an impact on number theory.

Set of anatomical organs involved in sexual and asexual [[Reproduction|reproduction]], also known as the genital system. Hormones, [[Pheromone|pheromones]] and other non-living substances are important accessories to it. In mammals, the external genitalia include the [[Penis|penis]] and [[Vulva|vulva]], and the gamete-producing gonads include the testicles and ovaries. In humans, during [[Sexual intercourse|sexual intercourse]], [[Semen|semen]] is ejaculated into the vagina, and sperm travel through the cervix to fertilize the ovum. Gestation in the uterus lasts about nine months, a period known as [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]], and ends with [[Childbirth|childbirth]]. The male reproductive system has one function, to produce and deposit sperm. The female system produces egg cells and protects and nourishes the offspring until birth.

Form of government in which political power rests with the public, typically through representatives, in contrast to an [[Absolute monarchy|absolute monarchy]] or a [[Democracy|direct democracy]]. The word derives from the Latin *res publica*, meaning "public thing" or "people's thing." The term took its meaning from the [[Constitution|constitution]] of the [[Roman Republic|Roman Republic]], established after the overthrow of the kings in 509 BC. That constitution included a senate of wealthy aristocrats, popular assemblies and a series of magistracies. As of 2017, 159 of the world's 206 [[Sovereign state|sovereign states]] used "republic" in their official names, though not all of them have elected governments. [[Cicero|Cicero]] translated the Greek *politeia* into Latin as *res publica*, and [[Renaissance|Renaissance]] scholars rendered it as "republic." During the Protectorate of [[Oliver Cromwell|Oliver Cromwell]], "commonwealth" was the most common term for the new monarchless state.

Socratic dialogue by [[Plato|Plato]], written around 375 BC, concerning [[Justice|justice]], the just [[City-state|city-state]] and the just man. Known in Greek as *Politeia*, it is Plato's best-known work and one of the most influential works of [[Philosophy|philosophy]] and political theory. [[Socrates|Socrates]] examines the meaning of justice and whether the just man is happier than the unjust man. After considering existing regimes, he proposes a series of hypothetical cities, culminating in Kallipolis, a [[Utopia|utopian]] city-state ruled by a class of philosopher-kings. The dialogue also addresses aging, love, the [[Theory of forms|theory of forms]], the immortality of the [[Soul|soul]], and the role of poetry in society.

Former state governing mainland China from 1912 until 1949. It was proclaimed after the [[Qing dynasty|Qing dynasty]] was overthrown in the Xinhai Revolution, with [[Sun Yat-sen|Sun Yat-sen]] as provisional president. After 1916 the country fragmented under regional warlords. The [[Kuomintang|Kuomintang]] under [[Chiang Kai-shek|Chiang Kai-shek]] achieved nominal reunification in 1928. Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931 and launched a full-scale invasion of China in 1937. The Kuomintang lost the [[Chinese Civil War|Chinese Civil War]] to the [[Chinese Communist Party|Chinese Communist Party]], and its government retreated to [[Taiwan|Taiwan]]. The Republic was a founding member of the [[United Nations|United Nations]].

Medieval and early modern maritime republic on the northwestern coast of [[Italy|Italy]], existing from 1099 to 1797. During the Late [[Middle Ages|Middle Ages]], it was a major commercial power in the Mediterranean and Black Sea, and between the 16th and 17th centuries it was one of Europe's major financial centers. It established colonies including [[Corsica|Corsica]], Monaco, southern [[Crimea|Crimea]], and the islands of [[Lesbos|Lesbos]] and Chios. In the early modern period, it lost many of these and shifted its focus to banking, becoming a long-lasting partner of the [[Spanish Empire|Spanish Empire]]. In practice the republic was an [[Oligarchy|oligarchy]] ruled by a small group of merchant families. Its navy won the Battle of Meloria against Pisa in 1284. The republic ended when the French First Republic under [[Napoleon|Napoleon]] conquered it and replaced it with the Ligurian Republic.

Country in northwestern Europe, comprising 26 of the 32 counties of the island of [[Ireland|Ireland]]. It has a population of about 5.5 million, and its capital and largest city is [[Dublin|Dublin]]. It is a unitary parliamentary republic with an elected president, who serves as largely ceremonial head of state, and a Taoiseach who leads the government. The Irish Free State was created with Dominion status in 1922, and the state was officially declared a republic in 1949. It joined the [[United Nations|United Nations]] in 1955 and the European Communities in 1973, and it is now a member of the [[European Union|European Union]]. It is also a founding member of the [[Council of Europe|Council of Europe]] and the [[OECD|OECD]]. Ireland follows a policy of military neutrality and is not a member of [[NATO|NATO]]. The [[Good Friday Agreement|Good Friday Agreement]] of 1998 led to cooperation between the Irish and Northern Irish governments on policy areas.

Short-lived sovereign country in [[North America|North America]], existing from March 2, 1836, to February 19, 1846. It emerged from the Texas Revolution, which began in October 1835 against [[Mexico|Mexico]]. The Mexican Congress never recognized its independence, and its southern and western borders remained disputed. The United States annexed the republic on December 29, 1845, making Texas the 28th state, and that annexation led to the [[Mexican–American War|Mexican–American War]]. [[Sam Houston|Sam Houston]] was elected as the republic's first president in 1836.
